The Diagonal of a Square is a fundamental concept in geometry used to determine the distance between two opposite vertices of a square. It is commonly expressed by the formula d = l√2 and is typically introduced to students during middle school, when they begin studying geometric properties and the Pythagorean Theorem.

This formula involves two main variables: d and l. The variable d represents the diagonal of the square, while l represents the length of one of its sides. Since a square has right angles, the diagonal can be found by applying the Pythagorean Theorem to the right triangle formed by two sides and the diagonal.

The study of diagonals and right triangles dates back to ancient civilizations, especially Greek mathematicians such as Pythagoras, who developed the theorem that relates the sides of a right triangle. These concepts became fundamental in geometry and were later formalized within Euclidean geometry around the 3rd century BC.

Because of its importance in geometric calculations, the Diagonal of a Square formula is an essential tool, widely used to determine distances, solve problems involving squares, and understand spatial relationships in both mathematics and real-world applications.
